diagrams.title: Neutrophilic Dermatoses by Morphology
diagrams.subtitle: A practical taxonomy for choosing the biopsy, workup, and first safety decision

children.name: Sweet syndrome
children.detail: Tender pseudovesicular plaques; dense upper-dermal neutrophils and edema.

children.name: Neutrophilic dermatosis of dorsal hands
children.detail: Sweet-spectrum localized to dorsal hands; pustulation/ulceration and secondary vasculitic change may occur.

children.name: Rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatitis
children.detail: Symmetric papules, plaques, nodules, or bullae in RA; dense dermal neutrophils without primary vasculitis.

children.name: Pyoderma gangrenosum
children.detail: Classic, bullous, pustular, vegetative, peristomal, postoperative, and genital variants.

children.name: Necrotizing neutrophilic dermatosis
children.detail: Sweet/PG spectrum mimicking necrotizing infection; frequently postoperative or hematologic.

children.name: Neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis
children.detail: Short-lived macules/thin plaques; neutrophils and leukocytoclasia without vasculitis.

children.name: Still/autoinflammatory urticarial eruptions
children.detail: Systemic phenotype may dictate IL-1–directed treatment.

children.name: Amicrobial pustulosis of folds
children.detail: Autoimmune-associated sterile pustules favoring folds, scalp, and periorificial sites.

children.name: Subcorneal pustular dermatosis
children.detail: Flaccid half-half pustules; subcorneal neutrophils; screen for IgA gammopathy.

children.name: Generalized pustular psoriasis
children.detail: Sterile pustules with systemic inflammation; distinguish from AGEP and infection.

children.name: Palisaded neutrophilic granulomatous dermatitis
children.detail: Early neutrophilic/vasculitic lesions evolve to palisaded granulomas.

children.name: Interstitial granulomatous dermatitis
children.detail: Interstitial histiocytes around altered collagen; rope-like cords or plaques.

root.name: Neutrophilic dermatoses
root.detail: Classify by dominant clinical morphology and histologic compartment; overlap is common.

citations.quote: Review classifies neutrophilic dermatoses by clinical and histopathologic pattern and emphasizes exclusion of infection and systemic associations.
Review defines neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis as transient, usually nonpruritic lesions with dermal neutrophilia, leukocytoclasia, and no vasculitis.
A 65-patient series supports reactive granulomatous dermatitis as an umbrella for IGD, PNGD, and related patterns with frequent systemic associations.

diagrams.title: Necrotizing Infection vs Neutrophilic Mimic
diagrams.subtitle: A dual-track emergency algorithm that avoids both delayed surgery and pathergy-driven harm

steps.prompt: Rapidly progressive painful erythema, bullae, purpura, ulceration, crepitus, shock, or systemic toxicity?
Treat as a possible necrotizing infection while evaluating in parallel
steps.detail: Immediate surgical/infectious-disease assessment, blood cultures, broad antimicrobials when indicated, laboratory resuscitation, and imaging only if it will not delay source control.

steps.prompt: Are there strong neutrophilic-disease clues: prior PG/Sweet, pathergy at procedure sites, multifocal symmetric lesions, sterile prior cultures, hematologic disease, G-CSF exposure, or worsening after debridement?
Obtain deep edge biopsy and tissue cultures; involve dermatology/dermatopathology urgently
steps.detail: Both infection and neutrophilic disease can coexist. Histology should be interpreted with cultures, imaging, operative findings, and serial trajectory.

branches.label: No infection evidence + compatible neutrophilic pathology

steps.detail: Prompt source control and antimicrobial therapy take priority. Reassess for a superimposed inflammatory reaction if lesions progress despite adequate source control.
Stop nonessential trauma/debridement, initiate specialist-directed immunosuppression while maintaining infection surveillance, and investigate associated hematologic/inflammatory disease.
Repeat/deeper sampling, broaden microbiology, and use multidisciplinary review. Do not let a single negative culture or nonspecific neutrophilic biopsy close the case.
Sweet, PG, NUD, pustular, and reactive granulomatous disorders still require infection exclusion proportional to risk.

International Delphi criteria for ulcerative pyoderma gangrenosum combine an ulcer-edge neutrophilic biopsy with validated clinical minor criteria.
